title: Next Week I Am
overview: This unit is about what happens next. You will read a timetable, book a seat and tell somebody your plan. You will learn four ways to talk about the future, and a test for choosing one. You will also hand things over: pass me the form, send her the ticket.
learningPath: Meet 30 words for travelling, handing over and future time.
Read a short text, an information page and a real notice.
Learn the timetable present: the train leaves at six.
Compare four futures, and use the test to pick one.
Give instructions with two things after the verb.
Choose to or -ing, and watch the meaning change.
Speak, write, and check every answer against the key.
Take the quiz, then record your unit assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 13. This unit is about what happens next.
You already know how to say what is happening now, and what happened before.
Now you will say what happens next week, and next month.
Start with the words for travelling.
A departure is a leaving. An arrival is a getting there.
The screen at a station shows the departure time and the arrival time.
A gate is the door you walk through before you get on a plane.
A platform is the long, flat place beside the train, where you wait.
A terminal is the big building where journeys start and end.
A transfer is the short journey between one part of a trip and the next.
Luggage is your bags. A booking is the seat you have arranged and paid for.
Now the words for handing things over.
Hand and pass are close. You hand somebody a form. You pass the salt.
Obtain means get. You see it on notices: obtain a ticket at the desk.
If you owe somebody money, you have not paid them yet.
Supply and provide both mean give people the thing they need.
Share means two people use one thing. Exchange means you give one and get another.
Then the words for agreeing to do something.
Promise, intend, hesitate, suggest, consider, deny.
I promise to call. I intend to leave early. I suggest waiting.
Now the grammar, and the big idea of this unit.
English has four ways to say what happens next.
The first one is new. Call it the timetable present.
A timetable is a list of times: when a train leaves, when a shop opens.
The train leaves at six twenty. The shop opens at nine.
That is the present simple, but the time is in the future.
Use it only for a fixed time on a timetable or a schedule.
Somebody else set that time. You did not.
The second way you already know: am, is, are plus the -ing form.
I am meeting the manager on Tuesday.
Use it for an arrangement you have made with a person.
The third way is going to.
I am going to book the seat tonight.
Use it for a decision you made before now, or for something you can see coming.
The fourth way is will.
I will call you when I arrive.
Use it for a decision you make as you speak, for a guess, and for a promise.
Here is the test. Ask yourself three short questions, in this order.
One. Is the time on a timetable? Then use the present simple.
Two. Did you fix it with a person, with a time and a place? Then use the -ing form.
Three. Did you decide before now, or can you see it coming? Then use going to.
If the answer is no to all three, use will.
Stop at the first yes. That is the whole test.
Next, instructions with two things after the verb.
Send me the form. Give her the ticket. Pass him the bag.
The person comes first, then the thing.
The person needs no small word in front of it.
You can turn it round, but then you need to or for.
Send the form to me. Give the ticket to her. Buy a ticket for me.
One rule always works. If the thing is it or them, use the second order.
Say give it to her, not give her it.
Last, verbs that take to and verbs that take the -ing form.
A few verbs take both, and the meaning changes.
I stopped to eat means I stopped so that I could eat.
I stopped eating means I do not eat any more.
Remember to book means do not forget. The booking is still to come.
I remember booking means the memory is in my head. I did it.
To points forward. The -ing form points back.
Work through the cards in order, then check every answer against the key.
Record yourself, listen back, and compare with the model.
You can do all of this alone. Start now.

words.meaning: The time when something goes away, or the act of going.
words.example: The departure is at ten tonight.
practice: Our departure time is printed on the ticket.
The screen shows every departure in time order.
What time is your departure?
A late departure means a late arrival.
words.tutor: Give me five departure times, one at a time, and let me say each one back in a full sentence.

words.meaning: The time when something gets to a place, or the act of getting there.
words.example: The arrival is at half past six.
practice: Write your arrival time on the form.
The arrival screen is near the exit.
What is the arrival time of the next bus?
A short delay moved the arrival to seven.
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a departure and an arrival, then check whether I used both words correctly.

words.meaning: The door at an airport where you go out to the plane.
words.example: Go to gate four.
practice: The gate closes twenty minutes before the plane leaves.
Which gate is it?
They changed the gate to number nine.
Wait near the gate and watch the screen.
words.starter: The gate for my plane is …
words.tutor: Tell me a gate number and a time, and ask me to say when I have to be there.

words.meaning: A big building where a journey starts or ends.
words.example: The bus stops outside the terminal.
practice: This airport has two terminals.
Which terminal does your plane leave from?
The terminal is open all night.
Walk through the terminal to the train.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a terminal in four sentences, and tell me if any sentence is not about a building.

words.meaning: A short journey from one part of a trip to the next part.
words.example: The transfer from the airport takes an hour.
practice: Book the transfer when you book the room.
Is the transfer included?
We have a two-hour transfer between the trains.
A late plane can lose you the transfer.
words.tutor: Give me a journey with two parts and ask me where the transfer is.

words.meaning: The bags and cases you take with you when you travel.
words.example: Put your luggage on the trolley.
practice: My luggage is heavy.
Keep your luggage with you at the gate.
How much luggage can I take?
The luggage arrived on a later plane.
words.tutor: Ask me three questions about luggage rules, and check that I answer in full sentences.

words.meaning: A seat, a room or a place that you have arranged and paid for.
words.example: I have a booking for two nights.
practice: Show your booking at the desk.
Can I change my booking?
The booking number is on the email.
She made the booking a fortnight ago.
words.tutor: Play the person at a desk. Ask me for my booking number, then ask me to change the booking.

words.meaning: The long, flat place beside a train, where people wait.
words.example: The train leaves from platform three.
practice: Which platform does it go from?
Stand behind the line on the platform.
They moved us to another platform.
The platform was full of people.
words.tutor: Tell me a platform number and a time, then ask me to repeat both back to you.

words.meaning: To put a thing into somebody's hand.
words.example: Hand the form to the person at the desk.
practice: Hand me your ticket, please.
She handed him the key.
I will hand it back tomorrow.
Hand the card to the driver.
words.tutor: Ask me to say four sentences with hand, two with the person first and two with to.

words.meaning: To move a thing from you to somebody near you.
words.example: Pass me the salt, please.
practice: Can you pass him the bag?
He passed the phone to his sister.
Pass the list to the next person.
Pass me that paper.
words.tutor: Ask me when I would say pass and when I would say hand, and tell me if my answer is clear.

words.meaning: To get something, often by asking for it.
words.example: You obtain a ticket at the counter.
practice: Where can I obtain a form?
She obtained the copy in one day.
You must obtain permission first.
Obtain the receipt before you leave.
words.tutor: Ask me to say the same sentence twice, once with get and once with obtain, and say which one sounds like a notice.

words.meaning: To have to pay somebody money that you have not paid yet.
words.example: You owe 20 for the extra bag.
practice: I owe her for the ticket.
How much do I owe?
He owed nothing after Friday.
We owe the shop for two months.
words.tutor: Play the person at a desk. Tell me an amount I owe, and ask me to repeat it back.

words.meaning: To give people the things they need, again and again.
words.example: The café supplies water for every table.
practice: They supply the towels and the soap.
Who supplies the paper here?
The office supplied us with a map.
We can supply a chair if you ask.
words.tutor: Ask me for two sentences with supply where the thing is given many times, not once.

words.meaning: To give somebody something that they need.
words.example: The station provides a free map.
practice: Please provide your address on the form.
They provide a hot meal on the train.
Can you provide a photo?
The clinic provided a later appointment.
words.tutor: Ask me three questions that start with Can you provide, and check my answers are full sentences.

words.meaning: To use one thing together with another person.
words.example: We share a table in the café.
practice: Can we share the taxi?
They shared the cost of the transfer.
I shared my list with her.
Two people share this desk.
words.tutor: Ask me what I would share on a journey and what I would not, and why.

words.meaning: To give one thing and get another thing back.
words.example: You can exchange the ticket for a later one.
practice: Can I exchange this for a bigger size?
We exchanged phone numbers.
She exchanged her seat with mine.
Exchange the form at the counter.
words.tutor: Play a shop assistant. Refuse my first request to exchange something, then let me ask again politely.

words.meaning: To say that you will certainly do something.
words.example: I promise to call you tonight.
practice: He promised to send the form.
Do not promise more than you can do.
She promised me a copy.
I promise I will be there.
words.tutor: Ask me for three promises about next week, and check that each one uses to plus a verb.

words.meaning: To have a plan in your head to do something.
words.example: I intend to leave at six.
practice: We intend to travel overnight.
What do you intend to do next?
She intends to book the seat today.
They did not intend to be late.
words.tutor: Ask me what I intend to do this month, then ask me one question about each answer.

words.meaning: To wait a moment because you are not sure.
words.example: Do not hesitate to ask.
practice: He hesitated before he said yes.
I hesitate to promise anything.
She hesitated at the gate.
Do not hesitate, because the shop closes at six.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a moment when somebody hesitated, in three sentences.

words.meaning: To offer an idea for somebody to think about.
words.example: I suggest taking the earlier train.
practice: She suggested a different platform.
What do you suggest?
He suggested that we share a taxi.
I suggest you book it tonight.
words.tutor: Give me a travel problem and ask me to suggest two answers to it.

words.meaning: To think carefully about something before you decide.
words.example: Consider the price before you book.
practice: We are considering an overnight train.
Did you consider the transfer time?
He considered leaving early.
Please consider my request.
words.tutor: Ask me what I am considering doing next month, and ask me for one reason.

words.meaning: To say that something is not true.
words.example: He denies taking the bag.
practice: She denied the mistake.
Do not deny it if it is true.
He denied that he was late.
They deny any problem with the booking.
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between deny and refuse, and correct me if I mix them.

words.meaning: The evening or the night of today.
words.example: I am booking the seat tonight.
practice: The train leaves at ten tonight.
Are you working tonight?
Tonight I intend to rest.
We arrive tonight, not tomorrow.
words.tutor: Ask me three questions about tonight, and check that I answer with a future form.

words.meaning: Happening once every day.
words.example: There is a daily bus to the terminal.
practice: The shop has a daily delivery.
She checks the screen daily.
A daily ticket costs less than four single ones.
The service is daily except Sunday.
words.tutor: Ask me to say four things I do daily, using the present simple each time.

words.meaning: Through the night, from the evening until the morning.
words.example: We took the overnight train.
practice: The bags stayed at the terminal overnight.
An overnight journey saves a day.
Can I keep the car overnight?
They travelled overnight and arrived early.
words.tutor: Ask me whether I would travel overnight, and ask me for two reasons.

words.meaning: Happening once every week.
words.example: The weekly market opens at eight.
practice: I have a weekly lesson.
She pays the rent weekly.
A weekly ticket is cheaper.
They send a weekly email.
words.tutor: Ask me what happens weekly where I live, and check I use the present simple.

words.meaning: Two weeks; fourteen days.
words.example: The booking closes in a fortnight.
practice: I am away for a fortnight.
We meet once a fortnight.
The form arrived a fortnight later.
A fortnight is longer than ten days.
words.tutor: Ask me how many days a fortnight is, then ask me what I intend to do in a fortnight.

words.meaning: Happening once every month.
words.example: The monthly meeting is on Tuesday.
practice: She pays a monthly amount.
There is a monthly bus card.
We do a monthly check of the tools.
The monthly list comes by email.
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between weekly, monthly and yearly, and give me one example of each.

words.meaning: Happening once every year.
words.example: The yearly check is in March.
practice: A yearly ticket costs less than twelve monthly ones.
They hold a yearly event.
My yearly holiday starts tonight.
The yearly form arrives in January.
words.tutor: Ask me to say one yearly thing and one monthly thing, both in the present simple.

words.meaning: From that time forward, and after it.
words.example: From Monday onwards the shop opens at eight.
practice: From tonight onwards I will walk to work.
The new time starts from April onwards.
From gate nine onwards, the gates are on the other side.
She worked there from 2019 onwards.
words.tutor: Ask me to finish this sentence three times: From next month onwards, I …

grammar.title: The timetable decides: the train leaves at six
grammar.explanation: A timetable is a list of fixed times: when a train leaves, when a shop opens. For a time on a timetable, English uses the present simple. The time is in the future, but the verb is not. You did not choose that time. The timetable did.
grammar.rule:
The train leaves at six twenty.
The next bus arrives at half past four.
The shop opens at nine and closes at six.
The lesson starts on Monday.
Our plane leaves at ten tonight.
Ask about it: What time does the train leave?
Say no: The ticket office does not open on Sunday.
Use it for trains, buses, planes, shops, offices, lessons and films.
Do not use it for your own plans.
Not: I go to the market tomorrow.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: The office (close) at five tomorrow.
Ask: is this a fixed time that somebody else set?
Yes. An office has opening times.
So use the present simple.
The subject is the office. That is one thing, like he or she.
So the verb takes -s.
Answer: The office closes at five tomorrow.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to drop the -s: The shop open at nine. English needs it here, because the shop is one thing. Write: The shop opens at nine.
grammar.tip: If somebody else fixed the time, the verb stays plain and present. Ask yourself: is it on a list of times?
grammar.practice:
Write the verb in the present simple.
1. The train (leave) at seven forty.
2. The shop (not open) on Sunday.
3. What time (the plane / leave)?
4. The lesson (start) at six every Monday.
5. Our bus (arrive) at the terminal at nine.
6. The ticket office (close) at nine tonight.
7. The weekly market (finish) at two.
8. (the last train / go) before twelve?
grammar.answers:
1. leaves. 2. does not open. 3. does the plane leave. 4. starts. 5. arrives. 6. closes. 7. finishes. 8. Does the last train go
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing not opens. A negative present simple needs does not plus the plain verb, so the -s moves onto does.
Item 3 catches people the same way: does the plane leave, never does the plane leaves.

grammar.title: Choosing between four futures
grammar.explanation: You now know four ways to talk about what happens next. They are not the same. Each one tells the listener how fixed the thing is. This card puts them side by side and gives you a test.
grammar.rule:
1. The timetable present: The train leaves at six.
Somebody else fixed the time.
2. Am, is, are plus -ing: I am meeting the manager on Tuesday.
You fixed it with a person.
3. Going to: I am going to book the seat tonight.
You decided before now, or you can see it coming.
4. Will: I will call you when I arrive.
You are deciding now, guessing, or promising.
The test. Ask three questions, in this order, and stop at the first yes.
Is the time on a timetable? Then use 1.
Did you fix it with a person, with a time and a place? Then use 2.
Did you decide before now, or can you see it coming? Then use 3.
No to all three? Use 4.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: Look at those clouds. It (rain).
Question one: is the time on a timetable?
No. Rain has no timetable.
Question two: did you fix it with a person?
No.
Question three: can you see it coming?
Yes. The clouds are right there.
So use going to.
Answer: It is going to rain.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to use will for everything, because it is short. Will is for a decision you make as you speak. If the seat is already booked, say: I am flying on Tuesday. Not: I will fly on Tuesday.
grammar.tip: Fixed by a timetable, fixed with a person, decided earlier, decided now. Four boxes, in that order.
grammar.practice:
Choose one: the present simple, am/is/are + -ing, going to, or will.
1. The night train (leave) at ten fifteen. It says so on the notice.
2. I (see) the doctor at nine on Thursday. The appointment card is here.
3. Look at that queue. We (miss) the transfer.
4. The phone is ringing. I (answer) it.
5. I (book) the room tonight. I decided this morning.
6. The shop (open) at eight tomorrow, like every day.
7. I promise I (send) you the form.
8. We (travel) overnight on Friday. The tickets came yesterday.
grammar.answers:
1. leaves. 2. am seeing. 3. are going to miss. 4. will answer. 5. am going to book. 6. opens. 7. will send. 8. are travelling.
The likeliest wrong answer is 4: writing I am going to answer it. You decided as the phone rang, so it is will. Going to needs a decision you had already made.
Item 8 is the other trap. The tickets came yesterday, so the arrangement is fixed with a person and a date, and that is the -ing form.

grammar.title: Send me the form, give it to her
grammar.explanation: Some verbs carry two things after them: the person, then the thing. Send me the form. Give her the ticket. The person comes first and needs no small word in front of it. You can turn the order round, but then the person needs to or for.
grammar.rule:
Person first, then the thing:
Send me the form.
Give her the ticket.
Pass him the bag.
Hand the driver your card.
Thing first, then to or for plus the person:
Send the form to me.
Give the ticket to her.
Buy a ticket for me.
Verbs that work like this: give, send, pass, hand, show, bring, lend, buy, tell.
One rule always works. If the thing is it or them, use the second order.
Say: Give it to her. Not: Give her it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: the keys / hand / the neighbour.
Order one is person, then thing. The person is the neighbour.
Hand the neighbour the keys.
Order two is thing, then to plus the person.
Hand the keys to the neighbour.
Both are correct.
Now make the thing a pronoun. The keys become them.
Only order two works: Hand them to the neighbour.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to add a small word before the person. Send to me the form is the commonest slip. English does not do that. Write: Send me the form, or Send the form to me.
grammar.tip: Person then thing, or thing then to. If the thing is it or them, always use to.
grammar.practice:
Write each instruction again in the other order.
1. Pass me the salt.
2. Give the ticket to her.
3. Send him the booking number.
4. Hand your form to the person at the desk.
5. Show me your luggage.
6. Buy a card for your sister.
7. Lend the map to Tomas.
8. Tell me the platform number.
grammar.answers:
1. Pass the salt to me. 2. Give her the ticket. 3. Send the booking number to him. 4. Hand the person at the desk your form. 5. Show your luggage to me. 6. Buy your sister a card. 7. Lend Tomas the map. 8. Tell the platform number to me.
Check every answer for a stray small word. Hand to me the form is never right.
Item 8 turns round as Tell the platform number to me, because the number is not a pronoun. If it were, only Tell it to me would work.

grammar.title: Stopped to eat, or stopped eating
grammar.explanation: A few verbs take both to and the -ing form. The two do not mean the same thing. To points forward, at the reason or the next step. The -ing form points back, at the thing itself or at a memory.
grammar.rule:
stop
I stopped to eat. I stopped so that I could eat.
I stopped eating. I do not eat any more.
remember
Remember to book. Do not forget; the booking is still to come.
I remember booking. The memory is in my head; I did it.
forget
I forgot to pay. I did not pay.
I will never forget paying. The memory stays.
try
Try to open it. Make the effort.
Try opening it. Test it, and see what happens.
go on
She went on to speak about the transfer. A new thing.
She went on speaking. The same thing, without stopping.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: I stopped (buy) a ticket, and then I got on the train.
Ask: did the person stop so that they could buy?
Yes. The buying came after the stopping.
That points forward, so use to.
Answer: I stopped to buy a ticket, and then I got on the train.
Now change it. I stopped buying a ticket would mean I no longer buy one at all.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write: I remember to close the gate last night. Last night is finished, so the memory form is needed. Write: I remember closing the gate last night.
grammar.tip: To looks forward. The -ing form looks back at the thing itself.
grammar.practice:
Write to plus the verb, or the -ing form.
1. We stopped (have) a coffee on the way.
2. Please remember (hand) the form to the desk.
3. I will never forget (arrive) at that terminal at night.
4. Try (ask) at the other counter; they may be quicker.
5. He stopped (work) at six and went home.
6. She forgot (book) the transfer, so we paid twice.
7. I remember (pass) him the keys, but he says I did not.
8. Try (send) it again if the first email fails.
grammar.answers:
1. to have. 2. to hand. 3. arriving. 4. asking. 5. working. 6. to book. 7. passing. 8. sending.
The likeliest wrong answer is 5: writing stopped to work. That would mean he stopped in order to work. He finished for the day, so the -ing form is right.
Items 4 and 8 both take the -ing form, because each one means test it and see, not make the effort.

readings.title: The evening before
readings.setting: A kitchen table, the evening before a journey
readings.passage:
Ana is going away for a fortnight. Tomorrow she travels.
Her friend Tomas sits at the table with her.
'What time do you leave?' he asks.
'The train leaves at six twenty,' says Ana. 'It is on the timetable.'
'That is early. What are you doing tonight?'
'I am meeting my sister at eight. We arranged it last week.'
Tomas looks at the papers on the table.
'And these?'
'That is my booking. I am going to print it after dinner.'
'Do you want a ride to the station?'
Ana stops. She did not expect that.
'Yes,' she says. 'Thank you. What do I owe you?'
'Nothing,' says Tomas. 'Hand me the address and I will be here at half past five.'
Ana passes him the paper. He reads it twice.
'Platform three,' he says. 'I know it.'
'The transfer is the hard part,' says Ana. 'I have forty minutes.'
'You will be fine. Take your luggage to the front of the train.'
Ana promises to send a message when she arrives.
Then she goes to look for her bags.

readings.title: How a departure screen works
readings.passage:
Every big station and every airport has a screen. It is called the departure screen.
The screen lists the departures in time order. The next one is at the top.
Each line shows four things. The time, where it goes, the platform or the gate, and a note.
The time on that screen is a timetable time. Staff write it as a plain time: the train leaves at six twenty.
The note is the part people miss. It may say On time, Delayed, or Boarding.
Boarding means the gate is open now. Go there. The gate closes before the departure time, often twenty minutes before.
Delayed means the departure has moved to a later time.
The platform or the gate is often empty until the last minute. Staff do not fix it until the train arrives.
So look at the screen, then look again five minutes later.
An arrival screen works the same way, but it lists the arrivals. People waiting for somebody read that one.
If you have a transfer, the arrival screen matters more. It tells you how long you really have.
Keep your booking on your phone and on paper. A screen goes dark; paper does not.
Ask a member of staff if a line does not make sense. That is what they are there for.

readings.title: Platform 3: notice and times
readings.passage:
NOTICE FOR PLATFORM 3
From Monday 6 April onwards, the weekly timetable changes.

DEPARTURES FROM PLATFORM 3
Coast service: leaves 6.20 in the morning, arrives 9.05. Daily.
Hill service: leaves 7.40 in the morning, arrives 10.30. Daily except Sunday.
Night service: leaves 10.15 at night, arrives 5.50 in the morning. Friday and Saturday only.

BOOKINGS
The ticket office opens at 5.30 in the morning and closes at 9 at night.
Outside those hours, obtain your ticket from the machine beside the gate.
Bring your booking number. Staff cannot print a ticket without it.

LUGGAGE
Two bags per person. Hand any extra bag to the desk at the end of the platform.
You pay for extra luggage at the desk, not on the train.

TRANSFERS
For the airport transfer, leave the platform by the far exit.
The transfer bus runs every twenty minutes from 6 in the morning onwards.

If your train is delayed, we exchange your ticket for the next service at no cost.
Ask at the desk. Do not hesitate, because the desk closes when the last train leaves.

comprehension.q: What time does Ana's train leave, and which platform does it go from?
comprehension.a: It leaves at six twenty, from platform three.
comprehension.why: Ana says the train leaves at six twenty. Tomas reads the paper and says platform three.

comprehension.q: Who is Ana meeting tonight, and when did she arrange it?
comprehension.a: Her sister, at eight. She arranged it last week.
comprehension.why: Ana says: I am meeting my sister at eight. We arranged it last week.

comprehension.q: Tomas gives Ana a ride to the station. How much does she owe him?
comprehension.a: Nothing. He says so when she asks.
comprehension.why: Ana asks what she owes. Tomas answers with one word: Nothing.

comprehension.q: What does the word Boarding mean on a departure screen?
comprehension.a: It means the gate is open now, and you should go there.
comprehension.why: The text says: Boarding means the gate is open now. Go there.

comprehension.q: Why does the text tell you to look at the screen again five minutes later?
comprehension.a: Because staff often do not fix the platform or gate until the last minute.
comprehension.why: The platform is added late, so the line you read first may still be empty.

comprehension.q: Why does the writer say to keep your booking on paper as well?
comprehension.a: Because a phone screen can go dark, and paper does not.
comprehension.why: The text says: A screen goes dark; paper does not. It is advice, not a rule.

comprehension.q: The text says a line may say Delayed. What does delayed mean here?
comprehension.a: It means the departure has moved to a later time.
comprehension.why: Delayed is the opposite of On time. The train or plane leaves later than the timetable time.

comprehension.q: You want to travel overnight on a Wednesday. Can you?
comprehension.a: No. The night service runs on Friday and Saturday only.
comprehension.why: The notice limits the night service to two days, so a Wednesday night train does not exist.

comprehension.q: It is five in the morning and you have no ticket. What do you do?
comprehension.a: Get the ticket from the machine beside the gate, using your booking number.
comprehension.why: The ticket office opens at 5.30, so at five it is shut. The notice sends you to the machine.

comprehension.q: You have three bags. What does the notice tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Hand the extra bag to the desk at the end of the platform, and pay there.
comprehension.why: Two bags per person are allowed. The third is extra, and extra luggage is paid for at the desk.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The train leaves at
speaking.instructions:
Say these six lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
The train leaves at six twenty.
The shop opens at nine and closes at six.
The next bus arrives at half past four.
The ticket office does not open on Sunday.
What time does the plane leave?
Does the last train go before twelve?
Now make six of your own.
Use a real timetable near you: a bus, a shop, a clinic.
Play back your recording.
Check one thing: did you say the -s on leaves, opens, arrives and closes?
Say any line again if the -s is missing.
speaking.tutor: Listen to six timetable sentences from me and tell me if any verb is missing its -s.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Which future?
speaking.instructions:
Read each question, then say the answer out loud with the right future form.
What time does your train go? Answer with the timetable: My train leaves at seven.
What are you doing on Friday? Answer with the arrangement: I am meeting a friend at six.
Who will pay for the transfer? Answer with a decision made now: I will pay.
Why are you at the desk? Answer with a plan already made: I am going to change my booking.
Record the four answers. Play them back.
Check: did you use four different forms, one in each answer?
If two of them are the same, do it again.
speaking.tutor: Ask me four questions about next week, then tell me which future form each of my answers used.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Listen and write the details
speaking.instructions:
Play Reading 3, the platform notice. Listen without looking at the page.
Listen for four details. Write each one down.
1. The time the night service leaves.
2. The days the night service runs.
3. The time the ticket office closes.
4. How many bags each person may take.
Now look at Reading 3 and check your four answers.
The answers are: 10.15 at night; Friday and Saturday; 9 at night; two bags.
Four out of four? Move on.
Fewer? Play it once more, and listen only for the ones you missed.
Then say the four details out loud, record them, and play them back.
speaking.tutor: Read the platform notice to me slowly, then ask me four questions about the times and the days.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Hand it over
speaking.instructions:
You are at a desk in a terminal.
Say each line out loud twice: once with the person first, once with the thing first.
Hand me your ticket. Hand your ticket to me.
Give her the booking number. Give the booking number to her.
Pass him the bag. Pass the bag to him.
Show me your form. Show your form to me.
Send them the receipt. Send the receipt to them.
Record all ten lines. Play them back.
Check: in the second line of each pair, did you say to?
If you dropped it, say that pair again.
If somebody is with you, let them be the person at the desk.
You do not need them. The model lines above are the other half.
speaking.tutor: Play the person at a desk. Ask me for four things, and tell me if I put the person and the thing in the right order.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Stopped to, stopped -ing
speaking.instructions:
Talk for one minute about a journey, real or made up. You may invent every detail.
Use at least four of these five:
I stopped to, I stopped -ing,
I remembered to, I forgot to,
I tried -ing.
Here is a model. Read it first, then say your own.
Last month I travelled overnight.
I stopped to buy water at the terminal.
I forgot to print my booking, so I tried asking at the desk.
They found it. I remember passing the man my phone.
After that I stopped worrying.
Record yourself. Play it back and count how many of the five you used.
Four or more is a pass. Under four, record it again.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my one-minute journey and tell me which of the five forms I used and which I missed.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Ask and answer about a booking
speaking.instructions:
Ask six questions about a booking. Then answer each one yourself, in a full sentence.
Model questions:
What time does the train leave?
Which platform is it?
How much luggage can I take?
Can I exchange this ticket?
Where do I obtain a ticket at night?
What time do you arrive?
Record the six questions and the six answers. Play it back.
Check two things.
Did every question start with a question word, or with does, do or can?
Did every answer use a future form or a timetable time?
If a question is missing does or do, say it again.
speaking.tutor: Ask me six questions about a booking, one at a time, and tell me if any answer is not a full sentence.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Your week, in four lines
writing.prompt: Write four lines about next week. Use one line for each day you choose. Use a different future form in at least three of the four lines. You may invent the whole week.
writing.model:
Monday: The bus leaves at 7.10, so I leave home at seven.
Tuesday: I am seeing the doctor at nine. The card is on the fridge.
Thursday: I am going to book the weekly ticket.
Saturday: I will rest, or I will walk to the market.
writing.criteria: Four lines. Each line starts with a day and a colon. At least three different future forms across the four lines. Every line ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Do one line first. Take Monday. Ask the three test questions from card 2, in order, and stop at the first yes. Write that form.
writing.extension: Add a fifth line for a day when you have nothing planned. Use will.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A message about a bag
writing.prompt: Somebody is bringing a bag to you. Write them a message of five sentences. Tell them where to go and what to hand over. Use at least four instructions with two things after the verb.
writing.model:
Hi. Thank you for doing this.
Go to the terminal and find the desk at the end of platform three.
Hand the person your name and the booking number.
Give them the small bag, not the big one.
Send me a message when it is done, and I will pay you back.
writing.starter: Hi. Thank you for doing this.
writing.criteria: Five sentences. Four or more instructions with a person and a thing after the verb. Each sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
writing.support: Write only the instructions first, one per line: Hand … Give … Send … Show … Then add the first and last sentence.
writing.extension: Rewrite two of your instructions in the other order, with to.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A notice for a place you know
writing.prompt: Write a short notice, like Reading 3. Choose a place you know: a shop, a clinic, an office, or a made-up one. Use three headings in capital letters, and put the times under each one.
writing.model:
OPENING TIMES
We open at 8 in the morning, daily.
We close at 6, except on Friday, when we close at 8.
COLLECTIONS
Hand your card to the person at the counter.
We cannot provide a copy without it.
FROM APRIL ONWARDS
The weekly delivery moves to Tuesday.
The monthly meeting stays on the first Monday.
writing.criteria: Three headings, all in capital letters. Two lines under each heading. Every sentence about a time uses the present simple.
writing.support: Copy the three headings from the model first. Then write only the two lines under the first one.
writing.extension: Add a fourth heading for what somebody should do if they are late.

writing.title: Writing 4 — What I intend to do
writing.prompt: Write six sentences about a plan. It can be a journey, a course, or a change at work or where you study. You may invent it. Use intend, promise, suggest, consider, and one sentence with stopped, forgot or remembered.
writing.model:
I intend to travel overnight next month.
I am considering the coast service, because it arrives early.
I promise to book it a fortnight before.
I suggest leaving the big bag at home.
Last year I forgot to print the booking, so this time I will do it tonight.
From April onwards I intend to travel weekly.
writing.criteria: Six sentences. All five verbs used: intend, promise, suggest, consider, and one of stopped, forgot or remembered. Each verb is followed by to or by -ing, not by both.
writing.support: Write the five verbs down the page first, one per line. Then finish each line.
writing.extension: Add one sentence that uses the same verb twice, once with to and once with -ing, and say how the meaning changes.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: departure, arrival, gate, terminal, transfer, luggage, booking, platform.
1. The train leaves from ____ three.
2. Put your ____ on the trolley.
3. Show your ____ number at the desk.
4. Go to ____ nine; the plane leaves in half an hour.
5. The ____ is the big building where the journey starts.
6. Our ____ time is ten tonight.
7. The ____ screen tells you when people get here.
8. The ____ from the airport takes an hour by bus.
activities.answers:
1. platform 2. luggage 3. booking 4. gate 5. terminal 6. departure 7. arrival 8. transfer
Eight out of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the word cards for the ones you missed. Five or fewer: read all eight cards again, then do this once more.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Four futures, sorted
activities.instructions:
Read each sentence. Write which of the four it is: timetable, arrangement, going to, or will.
1. The shop opens at eight tomorrow.
2. I am meeting the manager at four on Tuesday.
3. That bag is heavy. I will carry it for you.
4. I am going to change my booking this evening.
5. Our plane leaves at ten fifteen.
6. Look at the queue. We are going to miss the transfer.
7. I am having dinner with my sister on Friday.
8. I think it will rain later.
activities.answers:
1. timetable 2. arrangement 3. will 4. going to 5. timetable 6. going to 7. arrangement 8. will
Item 6 catches people out. Nobody arranged the queue, and you are not deciding as you speak. You can see it coming, so it is going to.
Six or more right: move on. Fewer: go back to card 2 and use the three test questions on each item.
activities.solo: Do items 1 to 4 with card 2 open beside you. Do items 5 to 8 with it closed.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Turn the order round
activities.instructions:
Write each instruction again in the other order.
1. Hand me the form.
2. Give the ticket to the driver.
3. Send her the booking number.
4. Pass the bag to him.
5. Show the desk your card.
6. Buy a coffee for me.
7. Lend me your pen.
8. Tell him the platform.
activities.answers:
1. Hand the form to me. 2. Give the driver the ticket. 3. Send the booking number to her. 4. Pass him the bag. 5. Show your card to the desk. 6. Buy me a coffee. 7. Lend your pen to me. 8. Tell the platform to him.
Check each one for a stray small word. Hand to me the form is the commonest slip, and it is never right.
Seven or eight right: move on. Fewer: read card 3 again.
activities.solo: Say each answer out loud before you write it. The wrong order usually sounds wrong first.

activities.title: Practice 4 — To or -ing
activities.instructions:
Write to plus the verb, or the -ing form.
1. We stopped ____ (buy) water at the terminal.
2. Remember ____ (hand) the form in before Friday.
3. I will never forget ____ (wait) six hours at that gate.
4. Try ____ (ask) at the other desk.
5. He stopped ____ (drive) when it got dark.
6. She forgot ____ (book) the transfer.
7. I remember ____ (give) him the keys.
8. Try ____ (open) the window; the room is hot.
activities.answers:
1. to buy 2. to hand 3. waiting 4. asking 5. driving 6. to book 7. giving 8. opening
Items 1 and 5 are the pair to study. In 1 the buying comes after the stopping, so it is to. In 5 the driving ended, so it is the -ing form.
Six or more right: move on. Fewer: read card 4, then do items 1, 3, 5 and 7 again.
activities.solo: For each item ask one question first: does the second verb come after the stopping, or does it end? Write your answer beside the item before you fill the gap.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the notice
activities.instructions:
Use Reading 3 only. Write a short answer to each question.
1. Which service does not run on Sunday?
2. How do you get a ticket at four in the morning?
3. What must you bring to the ticket office?
4. Where do you pay for an extra bag?
5. Which exit do you use for the airport transfer?
6. How often does the transfer bus run?
7. What happens to your ticket if the train is delayed?
8. When does the desk close?
activities.answers:
1. The hill service. 2. From the machine beside the gate. 3. Your booking number. 4. At the desk at the end of the platform. 5. The far exit. 6. Every twenty minutes, from 6 in the morning onwards. 7. They exchange it for the next service, at no cost. 8. When the last train leaves.
Every answer is in the notice. If you could not find one, read the notice again with only that question in your head.
activities.solo: Answer from memory first. Then open the notice and mark the ones you got right. The gap between the two scores shows what to read more carefully.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Your own timetable
activities.instructions:
Find a real timetable near you.
It could be a bus stop, a shop door, a clinic notice, or a screen on your phone.
Write five sentences from it, in the present simple.
1. The ____ leaves at ____.
2. The ____ opens at ____.
3. The ____ closes at ____.
4. The ____ does not run on ____.
5. What time does the ____ leave?
Then read all five out loud.
activities.answers:
There is no single key here, because your timetable is your own. Check three things instead.
One: every verb takes -s if the subject is one thing. The bus leaves, not the bus leave.
Two: item 4 uses does not plus the plain verb. Not: does not runs.
Three: item 5 uses does plus the plain verb. Not: does the bus leaves.
All three right in all five sentences is a pass.
activities.solo: If you cannot find a real timetable, invent one. Write four times on a piece of paper first, then write the sentences from it.

quizzes.q: Which sentence uses the timetable present correctly?
options: The train leaves at six twenty.
The train is leave at six twenty.
The train leave at six twenty.
The train will leaves at six twenty.
quizzes.a: The train leaves at six twenty.
quizzes.why: A timetable time takes the present simple, and one train takes -s: leaves. The train leave drops the -s. Is leave mixes two forms. Will never takes a verb with -s.

quizzes.q: You fixed a time with the doctor last week. What do you say?
options: I will see the doctor on Thursday.
I am seeing the doctor on Thursday.
I see the doctor on Thursday.
The doctor is going to see me, I think.
quizzes.a: I am seeing the doctor on Thursday.
quizzes.why: An arrangement made with a person takes am, is or are plus -ing. Will is for a decision you make as you speak. The present simple is for a timetable, not for your own appointment. The last one is a guess, not the fixed fact.

quizzes.q: Look at those clouds. Which sentence fits?
quizzes.why: You can see it coming, so going to is right. Rain has no timetable, so It rains soon does not work. Is raining tomorrow claims an arrangement nobody made. It rain has no verb ending at all.

quizzes.q: The bag looks heavy. You decide, as you speak, to carry it. What do you say?
options: I am going to carry it.
quizzes.why: A decision made as you speak takes will. Going to needs a decision you had already made. The present simple is for timetables. I am carrying it says it is happening now.
In the person-first order the person takes no small word. Send to me the form adds one. Send me it should be Send it to me, because the thing is a pronoun. The last one is not English word order.

quizzes.q: The thing is a pronoun. Which sentence is right?
quizzes.why: When the thing is it or them, use the to order. Give her it is the order English avoids. Give it her to puts the small word last. An instruction never takes -s, so Gives is wrong.

quizzes.q: I stopped eating. What does it mean?
options: I stopped so that I could eat.
I ate and then stopped for a rest.
I do not eat that any more.
quizzes.a: I do not eat that any more.
quizzes.why: The -ing form points back at the thing itself, so the eating ended. I stopped to eat is the one that means I stopped so that I could eat. The other two are not about stopping at all.

quizzes.q: Which sentence tells somebody not to forget?
options: I will never forget booking it.
quizzes.why: To points forward, so this one is about something still to do. The other three use the -ing form, which points back at a memory of something already done.

quizzes.q: The notice says the night service is Friday and Saturday only. You want to travel on a Wednesday night. What can you do?
options: Take the night service; it runs daily.
Wait on the platform for the night service.
Take a different service, or travel on Friday.
Buy a night ticket from the machine.
quizzes.a: Take a different service, or travel on Friday.
quizzes.why: The notice limits the night service to two days, so on a Wednesday it does not exist. Buying a ticket cannot create a train, and waiting on the platform will not either.

quizzes.q: What does a departure screen show that an arrival screen does not?
options: The time trains and planes go.
quizzes.a: The time trains and planes go.
quizzes.why: A departure screen lists the ones leaving. The arrival screen lists the ones getting here, so that is the wrong way round. Neither screen shows prices or staff names.

quizzes.q: From Monday onwards the shop opens at eight. What does onwards mean here?
options: From Monday, and after it too.
quizzes.a: From Monday, and after it too.
quizzes.why: Onwards means from that time forward, with no end given. It is not one day only, it is not earlier, and the sentence states no number of weeks.

quizzes.q: Which word means to give one thing and get another thing back?
quizzes.why: Exchange means you give one thing and get another. Provide and supply both mean give somebody what they need, and nothing comes back. Obtain means get.

teacherNotes.note: The four futures are the whole unit, and the one learners overuse is will, because it is short and it never changes shape. If a learner writes will everywhere, do not correct sentence by sentence. Ask the three test questions from grammar card 2 out loud, in order, and let them answer each one. Two rounds of that usually fixes it for good.

The timetable present feels wrong to many learners, because the time is in the future and the verb is not. Point at a real timetable rather than explaining it again. A bus stop, a shop door or a clinic notice does the teaching in five seconds, and Practice 6 is built for exactly that.

In this unit the -s on the verb carries real meaning: the shop opens, the train leaves. A dropped -s is the commonest error in Practice 6 and in Speaking 1. It is audible, so have the learner read their five sentences out loud rather than read them again silently.

Give her it sounds acceptable to some learners and wrong to most speakers, and it is a regional matter rather than a clear error. The rule that always works is the one on card 3: when the thing is it or them, use the to order. Everything else in that card is a choice between two correct orders, not a right and a wrong.

The tutor is a rehearsal partner here, not a marking service. It is useful for reading the platform notice aloud at different speeds, for asking six questions about a booking, and for checking whether a sentence describes a timetable or an arrangement. Every task in this unit carries its own answer key, so nothing depends on the tutor's opinion.

selfAssessment.statement: I can read a timetable and say when a train or a shop opens.
I can choose between will, going to, the -ing form and the timetable present.
I can listen to a short travel notice and write down the times and the days.
I can give an instruction with two things after the verb.
I can use to or -ing after stop, remember, forget and try.
I can ask questions about a booking, and answer the ones I am asked.
I can write a short plan or notice with headings and clear lines.

assignment.title: Next week, in your own words
assignment.instructions:
Make one recording and write one short card. You may invent every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about one minute.
Say what happens next week. Use all four futures, at least once each:
a timetable time, for example the bus leaves at seven,
an arrangement, for example I am meeting a friend on Tuesday,
a decision you already made, for example I am going to book it,
and a decision you make as you speak, a guess or a promise, for example I will call you.
Add one sentence with intend and one with suggest.
Play it back and count the four forms. If one is missing, record it again.
Part 2. The card.
Write six lines with the layout of Writing 1: a day, a colon, then the line.
Use at least three different future forms across the six lines.
Use two instructions with two things after the verb, for example: Send me the number.
Under the card, write one line that starts: This shows I can …
Check your card against the four criteria for Writing 1 before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and a written card
